title: Investigate life and work related problems using data and probabilities

lessons.title: Planning an investigation and collecting data
lessons.html:
Using data to investigate problems

Supervisors and team leaders often face questions that data can answer: Why are more cartons being rejected at the export inspection? Is one sizer lane producing more damaged fruit? Are injuries more common on certain shifts? A structured investigation gives reliable answers instead of guesses.

The investigation cycle

  1. Pose a question that can be answered with data.
  2. Plan: decide what data to collect, from whom or what, how and when.
  3. Collect data carefully and consistently.
  4. Organise and represent the data in tables and graphs.
  5. Analyse using summary measures.
  6. Interpret and conclude, then recommend action.

Populations and samples

The population is the whole group you want to know about, such as all cartons packed this week. A sample is the part you actually measure, such as 5 cartons from every pallet. Samples must be representative: if you only sample at the start of the shift, you may miss problems that appear when workers tire or machines heat up. Random sampling, where every item has an equal chance of selection, reduces bias.

Types of data

  • Categorical (qualitative): defect type, shift, variety, lane number.
  • Numerical (quantitative): discrete counts, such as number of defects, or continuous measurements, such as mass, temperature or Brix.

Collection tools

Use check sheets with tally marks for defects by type, data loggers for temperature, scales for mass and simple questionnaires for staff views. Design forms so they are quick to complete and include date, time, location and the name of the person recording.

lessons.title: Representing and summarising data
lessons.html:
Making data meaningful

Frequency tables

A frequency table shows how often each value or category occurs. Example of rejected fruit by defect type in one day:

DefectFrequencyPercentage
Blemish4840%
Bruising3630%
Wrong size2420%
Decay1210%
Total120100%

Choosing the right graph

  • Bar graph: compare categories, such as defects by type or lane.
  • Pareto chart: bars in descending order, showing the few causes that account for most problems. Here blemish and bruising together make up 70% of rejects, so they are the priority.
  • Histogram: distribution of continuous data, such as carton masses grouped into intervals.
  • Line graph: trends over time, such as cold room temperature or daily rejects.
  • Pie chart: parts of a whole.
  • Scatter plot: relationship between two variables, such as hours worked and error rate.

Measures of central tendency

For carton masses of 10.2, 10.4, 10.1, 10.6 and 10.2 kg:

  • Mean = sum ÷ count = 51.5 ÷ 5 = 10.3 kg.
  • Median = middle value in order (10.1, 10.2, 10.2, 10.4, 10.6) = 10.2 kg.
  • Mode = most frequent = 10.2 kg.

Measures of spread

Range = 10.6 − 10.1 = 0.5 kg. A process with small spread is consistent. Outliers, values far from the rest, should be investigated: they may be recording errors or real problems.

Misleading graphs

Be alert to graphs with truncated axes, uneven scales or missing labels that exaggerate differences.

lessons.title: Probability and drawing conclusions
lessons.html:
Probability

Probability measures how likely an event is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

Theoretical probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes. A fair die has a 1 in 6 chance of showing a 4.

Experimental (relative frequency) probability = number of times the event occurred ÷ number of trials. If 12 out of 400 sampled seed packets failed the germination test, the estimated probability of failure is 12 ÷ 400 = 0.03, or 3%.

Using probability for prediction

If 3% of packets fail, in a lot of 20 000 packets we would expect about 0.03 × 20 000 = 600 to fail. This helps decide whether a lot meets a customer's specification or needs further testing.

Combined events

For independent events, multiply probabilities. If the chance of a forklift being unavailable on any day is 0.1 and the chance of the weighbridge being down is 0.05, the chance of both on the same day is 0.1 × 0.05 = 0.005, assuming they are independent.

Risk in everyday life

Probability helps compare risks: the chance of hail damage in a season based on years of records, or the expected cost of not insuring equipment. Multiply probability by impact to estimate expected loss and decide whether prevention or insurance is worth the cost.

Drawing valid conclusions

  • Base conclusions on enough data; small samples can mislead.
  • Correlation does not prove causation. More errors on hot days may relate to fatigue, not the heat itself.
  • Consider other explanations and possible bias in how data was collected.
  • State conclusions clearly and recommend practical actions.

Reporting

A short investigation report includes the question, method, data summary with a graph, conclusion and recommendations. Example: 'Bruising accounted for 30% of rejects; most occurred on lane 3. Recommend inspecting lane 3 drop heights and padding.'

Key points

  • Follow the cycle: question, plan, collect, represent, analyse, conclude.
  • Samples must be representative; random sampling reduces bias.
  • Choose graphs to suit the data; Pareto charts show priority causes.
  • Experimental probability = occurrences ÷ trials.
  • Correlation does not prove causation; use enough data.
